name: Retting of flax and hemp fibres
note: Flax and hemp stalks are soaked in water or exposed to dew for weeks to break down the pectin that binds the woody core to the long fibers. This controlled fermentation must be watched carefully, as overretting weakens the fibers and underretting leaves too much woody material to separate.

name: Scutching: breaking fibres from woody core
note: After retting, the dried flax or hemp stalks are broken and then beaten over a board with a wooden blade, so the brittle woody core falls away and the long bast fibres remain. Flails give a crude mechanised version of the same beating. Quality depends on beating firmly enough to free the core without tearing the fibres.

name: Hackling: combing and grading fibres
note: After scutching, hackling pulls the fibre bundle through a series of boards set with metal pins, from coarse to progressively finer. Each pass combs out more short, tangled fibre (tow) and straightens the long fibre (line). The long line is what can be spun into fine thread, while the tow makes coarser yarn.

name: Cotton gin: separation of seed from fibre
note: Wire hooks on rotating cylinder brush cotton past fixed blade, seeds fall away, reduces hand ginning labour by factor of fifty

name: Carding: opening and aligning fibres
note: Paired toothed cards open and align cleaned fibre into a roll for spinning. This is distinct from ancient combing and requires a repeatable field of fine teeth.

name: Combing: alignment of long fibres
note: Combs of progressive fineness remove short fibres and neps, produces smoother yarn than carding, only for long-staple fibres like flax and worsted

name: Gilling: parallel alignment after combing
note: Two finely-toothed combs slide over fibres held in roller nips, removes remaining short fibres and duplicates combing process

name: Drawing: fibre blending and extension
note: Drawing feeds several slivers or rovings together (doubling) and stretches them between pairs of rollers, each pair turning faster than the one before. Doubling averages out thick and thin places so the strand becomes even, and different fibres or colours can be blended this way. The amount of stretching is called the draft, and an even strand is needed for even yarn.

name: Roving frame: fibre attenuation and twist
note: Between carded fibre and finished yarn there is a stage called roving: a loose, thick strand with just enough twist to hold together. In the roving frame, pairs of rollers turning at increasing speeds stretch the fibre strand thinner, and a rotating arm called a flyer twists it and winds it onto a bobbin. The spinning frame can only finish a strand that is already even and thin enough, so this step feeds it.

name: Sliver: card output and sliver can
note: A sliver is a loose, untwisted rope of carded fibres, the product that comes off a carding machine. It is coiled into a tall can so it can be fed to the drawing frame, which evens it out before spinning. It needs carding, which opens and aligns the fibres. With no twist the sliver is weak, so it must be handled gently and kept from tangling.

name: Flyer: the earliest spinning frame component
note: U-shaped guide of twisted metal, draws fibre at constant rate while imparting twist, basis of all frame spinning before the ring frame

name: Bobbin and flyer assembly: early spinning
note: Bobbin holds spun yarn, flyer guides it at controlled rate, differential speed creates twist, foundation spinning geometry before ring frame

name: Cap frame spinning
note: Wooden spindle with metal cap, flyer rotates with spindle, early frame for coarser counts, easier to wind than flyer and bobbin

name: Ring frame: the dominant spinning geometry
note: Traveller slides on fixed ring, spindle rotates below, continuous yarn formation, allows higher speeds and finer counts, gradually displaced cap frame from 1870s

name: Spinning mule: draw-twist-wind
note: Carriage moves in and out, spindles move back and forth, intermittent action allows finer yarns than ring frame, handcraft for winding, steam-powered versions still require skill

name: Throstle: continuous drawing and twist
note: Ring frame with spindle speed matched to roller draft, fully continuous, better for coarser counts than mule, easier to automate than mule

name: Doubling frame: twisting multiple yarns
note: Two or more bobbins feed into single twist spindle, creates plied yarn for strength and appearance, essential for warp threads

name: Yarn count standardisation
note: Count is length per weight unit, English Cotton Count is 840 yards per pound, essential for yarn specification and trade

name: Twist insertion control
note: Quantified twist specification measured as turns per unit length and S/Z direction. Ordinary spinners already control twist by feel; this node standardises measurement so workshops can reproduce a specified yarn.

name: Shed: warp separation for pick insertion
note: The shed is the opening made between two sets of warp (lengthwise) threads, raised and lowered, through which the shuttle carries the weft (crosswise) thread. Every weaving machine, however complex, is built on this idea. The weaver needs a way to lift some warp threads and not others, then change over, so the weft interlocks. A shed that is too narrow catches the shuttle and breaks threads.

name: Heddle: warp thread carrier and riser
note: A heddle is a loop of metal or string that holds one warp thread. Raising and lowering a row of heddles lifts chosen warp threads to open the shed for the weft. In early looms the heddles were made and tied by hand, which is slow work. The heddles must be uniform and strong, or threads catch and break, and the pattern of which threads go on which heddle fixes the weave.

name: Shaft: harness frame assembly
note: Wooden frame holding heddles, multiple shafts create different shed patterns, basic hand loom has four shafts for tabby and twill

name: Dobby head: mechanical shed control
note: Pegged barrel or chain cam controls shaft raising, each peg or link controls one pick, allows complex patterns without Jacquard cost

name: Jacquard head: automatic pattern control
note: Each warp thread on independent hook, punched cards control individual hooks, enables arbitrary patterns, complex and expensive

name: Jacquard cards: pattern storage and control
note: Punched cards laced together, each row represents one pick, hole position controls hook, complex patterns require hundreds of cards

name: Shuttle: weft carrier and timing
note: Pointed boat-shaped carrier holding bobbin, travels through shed, must be timed to stop at selvage, critical for loom speed

name: Picking: mechanical shuttle propulsion
note: Picking is the throw that sends the shuttle, which carries the weft thread, through the gap between the warp threads. In a power loom a rotating cam moves arms called picker sticks that strike the shuttle at each end and drive it across, replacing the weaver's hand throw. It needs hard, accurately fitted metal parts, since the shuttle is struck over and over, and it lets looms run much faster than a person can throw.

name: Take-up: woven cloth winding
note: The take-up motion winds finished cloth onto a roller as it is woven. A graduated drum turns at a controlled rate that sets how closely the weft threads are packed, and it compensates for warp tension so the cloth does not bunch up. It works together with the let-off, which feeds warp. It needs a ratchet or gear drive made to fine tolerance. A fault gives uneven cloth.

name: Let-off: warp feed control
note: The let-off motion feeds warp threads from the warp beam as weaving uses them up. A brake on the beam keeps the tension constant as the yarn unwinds, so the cloth is even and threads do not break. It is synchronised with the take-up motion that winds up the cloth. It needs a weighted lever or friction brake. Too tight and threads snap; too loose and the weave is slack.

name: Temple: cloth width maintenance
note: The temple is a frame with sharp points that grips both edges of the cloth as it is woven and holds it to full width. Without it the weft thread pulls the warp inward (draw-in) and breaks threads at the edge. It expands as the cloth comes forward. It needs small, sharp, polished points and a precise mount. Points that are too coarse tear the edges.

name: Warp sizing: fibre stiffening
note: The warp is the set of long threads held in the loom, and weaving rubs them repeatedly against the loom parts, so weak yarn frays and breaks. Sizing coats the warp with a paste, often of starch, that lays down loose fibre ends and stiffens the thread so it resists rubbing. The size is washed out of the finished cloth. Fast weaving breaks unsized thread constantly, so sizing is needed for high speeds.

name: Warping mill: warp thread length setting
note: A rotating frame measures equal warp lengths and transfers them under controlled tension to the loom beam; the project adapts existing beam and winding practice.

name: Beam: warp holder and tension
note: The beam is a heavy wooden roller on which the warp threads are wound before weaving. A large diameter keeps the tension even from the first turn to the last, and it is the main support structure of the loom. It needs strong, straight timber, carefully turned. A bent or uneven beam causes uneven tension, and uneven tension makes flawed cloth.

name: Selvedge: woven cloth edge
note: Finished edge from shuttle reversing, tighter weave than body, essential for quality cloth, achieved by plain weave turn-around

name: Automatic loom: self-threading shuttle
note: Empty shuttle automatically ejected and threaded shuttle inserted, eliminates hand threading, increases speed and reduces downtimes

name: Automatic bobbin changer: weft supply
note: Automatic supply of full bobbins when current runs out, eliminates manual bobbin replenishment, essential for unattended running

name: Stocking frame: hosiery machine
note: Reciprocating needles hold loops, springs pull down, needles rise to throw loop, produces high-quality hosiery, skilled operator control

name: Circular knitting machine: tubular production
note: A knitting machine with a ring of needles on a rotating bed that makes cloth as a continuous tube, ideal for stockings and underwear. The motion is truly circular, so production runs without stopping, and coarse or fine gauges (needle spacing) can be chosen. It needs the stocking frame as a base and needles made to fine tolerance. A single bent needle ladders the fabric.

name: Warp knitting: sheet production
note: Multiple yarn guides feed warp-wise, creates sheet fabric instead of tube, less stretch than weft knitting, high speed possible

name: Latch needle: self-contained knit mechanism
note: Self-closing latch eliminates spring requirement, lighter pressure, enables higher gauge and finer yarns, invention transformed knitting

name: Scouring: removal of grease and soil
note: Hot alkali bath removes natural oils and dirt, essential preparatory step for dyeing and bleaching, caustic or soap-based

name: Fulling: cloth densification
note: Mechanical or chemical treatment matts fibres, shrinks and densifies cloth, essential for wool cloth, water-powered fulling mills

name: Milling: extended fulling
note: Milling is a longer fulling: woollen cloth is beaten and pressed wet, so the scales on the fibres lock together and the cloth shrinks into a thick, dense, felt-like fabric. It needs fulling equipment and hot water or soap. Cloth shrinks a lot, so it must be woven loose to begin with. Over-milling makes it stiff and brittle.

name: Raising: fibre napping
note: Raising pulls the ends of fibres up out of woven cloth to make a soft surface called a nap, as on blankets and woollen cloth. By hand it is done with teasels, the dried prickly heads of a plant, drawn across the damp cloth. A machine carries teasels or wire brushes on a rotating cylinder and passes the cloth over it. Fulled cloth is needed first, and the nap is usually trimmed afterwards to even it.

name: Cropping: nap trimming
note: Rotating cylinders with sharp blades trim raised nap to uniform height, creates smooth surface, high speed continuous operation

name: Shearing: precision cutting
note: Shearing cuts the pile of cloth to an even height using a stationary blade against a rotating grooved drum, like a lawn mower. It gives the smooth surface of velvet and other pile fabrics. It needs cropping (trimming nap) and blades ground to fine tolerance. A blade set wrongly cuts holes in the cloth or leaves ridges.

name: Calendering: surface pressing
note: Calendering passes cloth between heated rollers under controlled pressure so the surface is compacted and shines. It gives smoothness and sheen, and it is essential for cotton satins. It needs heavy rollers ground true and a source of heat. Too much heat or pressure scorches or flattens the cloth, and the finish washes out unless it is set.

name: Mercerising: caustic treatment
note: Caustic soda under tension swell and align cotton fibres, increases lustre and dye uptake, becomes permanent feature of premium cotton

name: Singeing: flame removal of nap
note: Open flame across cloth surface burns fine fibres, produces smooth finish, replaces hand holding over candle with continuous flame

name: Desizing: size removal
note: Desizing removes the starch size that was applied to warp threads to strengthen them for weaving. It is done with enzymes or chemicals. It must come before dyeing and finishing, because the size blocks dye and makes uneven colour. It needs scouring and a hot vessel. Leaving size in the cloth gives blotchy dye and a stiff, spotty finish.

name: Bleaching by sunlight: oxidative whitening
note: Linen and other plant fibres start out yellowish or grey. Bleaching by sun means spreading the cloth on grass and keeping it wet, so that sunlight, moisture and air slowly destroy the colouring matter. It needs open land, clean water and a lot of time, which makes it the slowest method. It is the gentlest on the fibres, and was the traditional treatment for linen.

name: Bleaching by chlorine: rapid whitening
note: Chlorine water or bleach powder oxidises colour bodies, fastest industrial method, some fibre damage especially to cotton

name: Bleaching by hydrogen peroxide: mild oxidation
note: Milder than chlorine, leaves no toxic residue, gentler on fibres, requires careful pH control, becomes preferred method by 1920s

name: Dyeing in fibre: pre-spin colouration
note: Loose fibres or cards dipped in dye bath, blends different coloured fibres before spinning, essential for heathers and mixtures

name: Dyeing in yarn: skein colouration
note: Dyeing yarn in skeins: loops of yarn are hung in a dye bath so the colour penetrates every thread before weaving. It gives solid colours and woven patterns. The dye liquor must reach all the yarn evenly, or colour is patchy, so skeins are turned. It needs a vessel, heat and dyes with mordants. It is essential for solid-colour fabrics.

name: Dyeing in piece: woven cloth colouration
note: Folded cloth in dye bath, most efficient use of dye, requires careful handling to avoid creases, standard for finished fabric

name: Dyeing in garment: finished good colouration
note: Finished garment dipped in vat, enables custom colouration, risk of shrinkage, labour-intensive due to garment complexity

name: Block printing: carved design application
note: Block printing applies a design to cloth by dipping a hand-carved wooden block with a raised pattern in dye and stamping it again and again. It needs wood, carving skill, dye thick enough not to run, and cloth. Making the design blocks takes a great deal of labour, and every colour needs its own block; alignment between blocks is the hard part.

name: Roller printing: engraved cylinder application
note: Engraved copper roller applies pattern continuously, replaces block printing, enables fine detail and high speed, expensive engraving

name: Screen printing: mesh stencil application
note: Silk or other mesh with photographic emulsion stencil, squeegee forces dye through, emerges in 1920s for fine art and textile printing

name: Resist dyeing: pattern preservation
note: Wax, starch paste, tied thread, or clay blocks dye from selected areas; remove the resist after the dye bath to reveal the pattern. Each resist must survive the bath without bleeding into the fibre.

name: Discharge printing: dye removal
note: Bleaching agent printed onto dyed cloth removes colour, creates light patterns on dark background, requires proper discharge agents

name: Waterproofing: moisture resistance
note: Oil or wax coating repels water, essential for outdoor wear, reduces breathability, various formulations tested in early 20th century

name: Flameproofing: combustion resistance
note: Chemical treatment slows combustion, essential for children's wear and upholstery, various formulations with durability challenges

name: Mothproofing: insect resistance
note: Treating wool so that moth larvae will not eat it. The chemicals are toxic and repel the insects; some old formulations include arsenic compounds, which are dangerous to workers and wearers. It is essential for wool stored for long periods. It needs a chemical source such as coal tar benzene extracts. The protection wears off and must be renewed.

name: Permanent press: wrinkle resistance
note: Resin cross-linking sets cloth shape, major innovation in 1930s-1940s, requires formaldehyde chemistry and heat treatment

name: Flax cultivation and fibre
note: Long bast fibres from flax plant, strongest vegetable fibre, linen production base, Mediterranean and European cultivation

name: Hemp cultivation and fibre
note: Hemp is a tall plant grown for the fibre in its stem. It is like flax but coarser and stronger, and is used for rope and canvas. The stems are retted (soaked so the woody part rots away from the fibre) and then beaten to free the fibre. It needs farmland and water for retting. Retting pits smell badly and can foul streams.

name: Jute cultivation and fibre
unheld_reason: Bengal jute is outside the modelled start regions
note: Indian river plant, coarse bast fibre, cheap and fast-growing, bagging and carpet use, emerges as industrial fibre in 19th century

name: Ramie cultivation and fibre
note: Ramie is an Asian plant whose stem bark gives a fine, strong, lustrous bast fibre (plant fibre from the inner bark). It is grown in China and India. The fibre is held together with gum that is hard to remove, and this difficult processing limits its adoption. It needs a warm, wet climate and hand labour for stripping.

name: Wool: sheep fibre
note: Protein fibre from sheep, natural crimp and elasticity, warmth and moisture absorption, Mediterranean and Northern European production

name: Worsted: combed wool yarn
note: Worsted is yarn spun from long-staple wool fibres that have been combed so the fibres lie parallel. It is smooth and strong, and is used for fine suiting. It needs wool of long fibre and combing to align it. Short, carded wool makes a different, fuzzier yarn. It was a speciality of the English West Country.

name: Mohair: angora goat fibre
unheld_reason: Anatolian angora goat fibre is outside the modelled start regions
note: Mohair is the fibre from the Angora goat, a breed originating around Ankara in Turkey. It is lustrous and strong, and used for luxury cloth. Production was long a monopoly of the region around Istanbul, and exporting the goats was forbidden. It needs the goats and a suitable pasture. Supply was restricted, so cloth was dear.

name: Cashmere: goat undercoat fibre
unheld_reason: Kashmir goat fibre is outside the modelled start regions
note: Cashmere is the fine, soft undercoat of goats raised in Mongolia and the Himalaya. It grows beneath the coarse outer hair and is combed or sheared and sorted by hand. It is extremely fine and warm, a luxury fibre. Kashmir was the trading centre. The animals give little fibre each, so it is scarce and costly.

copy_visibility_reason: The silk thread reveals nothing about the worm, the mulberry or the reeling of the cocoon; the secret was kept for centuries until monks are said to have smuggled eggs to Byzantium.
name: Silk: cultivated fibre
note: Silk is a protein fibre spun by silkworms in making their cocoons. It is a single continuous filament, lustrous and strong, and expensive. Production in Asia was long guarded so the methods did not travel. The founder cannot get silk without silkworms and mulberry leaves to feed them. Silk is a cultivated fibre, unlike wool or flax gathered from animals or fields.

name: Sericulture: silk production
note: Sericulture is silk farming: silkworms are raised on mulberry leaves, then their cocoons are stifled (killed with heat so the moth does not break out and cut the filament) and unwound; degumming removes the sericin gum that coats the thread. It is very labour-intensive. It needs silk stock, mulberry trees and skilled workers. Chinese and Indian expertise remained long unmatched.

name: Wild silk: non-cultivated production
note: Wild silk comes from the cocoons of silk moths that live in the wild, such as the Tussar and Muga silks of India and China. The filament is shorter and darker in colour than cultivated silk, and the cocoons are harder to unwind. It needs sericulture methods adapted to the wild moths. It is cheaper than cultivated silk but coarser.

name: Rayon by nitration: cellulose nitrate
note: Cellulose nitrate dissolved and extruded, first artificial fibre, flammable and unstable, replaced by safer cupro rayon

name: Rayon by cupro: copper-ammonia process
note: Cellulose in copper-ammonia complex spun through air, smoother than viscose, excellent silk-like lustre, emerges in 1890s

name: Rayon by viscose: alkali-carbon disulfide process
note: Most important rayon process, versatile and scalable, controls properties by coagulation bath, dominant by 1920s

name: Rayon by acetate: cellulose acetate
note: A fibre made by dissolving cellulose acetate (cellulose treated with acetic acid) and spinning it directly through fine holes, rather than regenerating plain cellulose as other rayons do. It is safer and easier than cupro rayon. It needs the cellulose acetate plastic and chemical plant. It is weaker than other rayons when wet and melts under a hot iron.

name: Nylon 6,6: polyamide synthesis
note: First fully synthetic fibre from petroleum, extraordinary durability and elasticity, DuPont patented 1935, launched 1940

name: Polyester: terylene synthesis
note: Polyethylene terephthalate condensation, extremely versatile, crease resistance, ICI developed pre-1950 but mass production post-war

name: Acrylic: polyacrylonitrile fibres
note: A synthetic fibre made by polymerising acrylonitrile (joining many small molecules into long chains), then dissolving the polymer and spinning it. It feels like wool and holds shape. It needs addition polymerisation and a supply of acrylonitrile from refined petroleum. Controlling the reaction and finding a solvent for the polymer are the hard parts.

name: Glass fibre: silica filament
note: Fine threads drawn from molten glass. Because glass drawn into thin fibres is strong and does not burn, it is used in insulation, reinforcement and heat-resistant cloth. The glass must be melted at very high temperature and pulled quickly into filaments through tiny holes. It needs a furnace of regenerative type for sustained heat. Broken fibres can irritate skin and lungs.

name: Asbestos cloth: fire-resistant fabric
note: Woven asbestos fibres, extreme heat resistance to 1100C plus, essential for protective wear and insulation, long-term health consequences unknown

name: Eye-pointed needle: self-threading sewing
note: A needle with its eye at the point instead of at the blunt end. As it goes through the cloth it pulls the thread with it in a loop, so the machine need not thread it from behind. Sewing machines depend on it. It needs steel wire drawn fine and a punch or drill that can make a tiny eye at the tip. Eyes that are rough cut the thread.

copy_visibility_reason: The stitch itself is visible in the seam and can be pulled apart, but the shuttle and the needle timing sit inside the machine head.
name: Lockstitch: two-thread interlocking
note: A stitch made with two threads: a needle thread passes through the cloth and its loop interlocks with a thread from a bobbin underneath. The two lock in the middle of the cloth, so the seam looks the same on both sides and is strong. The timing of the hook and needle and the tension on both threads must be exact. It is the most important sewing machine invention.

name: Chain stitch: thread-only interlocking
note: A stitch made with a single thread: the needle thread forms a loop that is caught by the next loop, like a chain. It was used in early machines and still serves special purposes. It needs an eye-pointed needle and a looper made to fine tolerance. It is less strong than lockstitch, because pulling the end unravels the whole seam.

name: Overlock: edge-covering stitch
note: A stitch that binds several threads over the raw edge of cloth, preventing fraying and sealing the edge. The machine sews, trims and covers in one pass. It needs the chain stitch mechanism extended with loopers for several threads. It is used on knitted garments and seam edges. Setting the tensions for multiple threads is difficult.

name: Buttonhole machine: eyelet cutting and binding
note: A machine that cuts a buttonhole slit in cloth and at the same time binds its edges with stitching so they do not fray. It replaces hand work and makes mass production of shirts possible. It needs an eye-pointed needle and a mechanism made to fine tolerance to control the cutter and the stitching. A badly bound hole frays quickly.

name: Cutting table: stacked cloth cutting
note: A large flat table with an edge, on which many layers of cloth are stacked and cut to the same pattern together. It lets many garment pieces be cut from a single cutting, saving labour. It needs a smooth, long, level table and sharp shears. Cutting too thick a stack makes the lower layers inaccurate.

name: Band knife: reciprocating cloth cutter
note: A cutting machine with an endless blade, driven by a motor in a reciprocating movement, that cuts through a thick stack of cloth. The cutter follows a pattern template or a drawn line. It replaces hand scissors and speeds cutting a great deal. It needs the cutting table, a reliable electric motor and blades ground to fine tolerance. A blunt blade frays the cut edge and drags the cloth.

name: Pattern grading: multi-size scaling
note: Scaling a master pattern to several sizes, so that garments fit a range of bodies without being designed one by one. Ratio grading means each measurement is increased by a proportion, not by a fixed amount. It is essential for ready-to-wear clothing. It needs standard pattern cutting and sizing systems based on body measurements. Poor grading gives garments that fit the middle size but no other.

name: Sizing systems: body measurement standardisation
note: A body-measurement survey tied to standard units and reusable garment patterns. The project establishes sample tables and workshop practice; it does not assume modern population-wide sizes.

name: Paper pattern: home sewing pattern
note: Printed pattern pieces and instructions, mass-market product, Butterick patterns emerge in 1860s, enables home dressmaking

name: Zip fastener: metal hook closure
note: Interlocking metal teeth on two tapes, slider engages hooks, invented in 1890s but refined in 1920s for widespread adoption

name: Press stud: snap fastener
note: A fastener made of four pieces of metal: two form a ball and socket that snap together under light pressure and pull apart on a firm tug. It is easier than buttons for infant wear. It needs brass or similar metal stamped and shaped to close tolerance, because a loose fit pops open and a tight one is hard to open.

name: Hook and eye: wire fastener
note: A matched pair of bent-wire pieces: a hook and a closed eye that it catches, each sewn to a garment edge so the garment can be closed and opened again. The wire must be drawn to a consistent diameter, and the pieces bent to a uniform shape. It needs a wire drawing bench. Poor hooks bend open and let go.

name: Elastic: rubber thread
note: Rubber covered thread or cord, recoverable stretch, essential for undergarments and sportswear, emerging in early 20th century

name: Corset: rigid body support garment
note: A fitted, boned or corded support bodice built from measured patterns. This introduces a specific rigid garment rather than treating all body-support clothing as one invention.

name: Brassiere: supportive undergarment
note: Elastic-based support without rigid boning, emerges in 1910s-1920s as alternative to corset, major innovation in women's comfort

name: Ready-to-wear: mass-produced garments
note: Factory-made garments in standard sizes, replaces bespoke tailoring for most consumers, emerged mid-19th century in America

name: Sewing machine: domestic version
note: Human-powered treadle or hand crank, complex motion conversion, Singer and others dominated market, transformed home sewing

name: Sewing machine: industrial version
note: Steam or electric powered, higher speeds and heavier fabrics, multiple machines linked by belts, factory standard from 1870s

name: Rope laying: strand twisting
note: Rope laying is twisting three or more yarns together into a strand, and strands together into a rope. The twist in opposing directions at each stage locks the rope so that it does not unravel and shares load among fibres. It needs fibre, such as hemp, and a long walk or machine for twisting. The basic construction of all ropes. A rope twisted too loosely is weak; too tightly, it is stiff.

name: Ropemaking machine: mechanised twisting
note: A machine of rotating frames that twists strands into rope, usually in water-powered mills. It makes continuous rope of consistent quality and great length. It needs rope laying methods, a power source and metal parts made to fine tolerance. Hand ropewalks, long sheds where rope is twisted by hand, produce far less.

name: Cordage for paperboard production
note: Cord made from paper pulp, twisted into a rope and used as an intermediate product for paperboard and containers. It needs rope laying methods and paper pulp. It gives a strong, cheap string where fibre rope would be wasteful. Moisture weakens it, and it is not for use where it would get wet.

name: Vegetable tanning: oak bark curing
note: Tannins from oak bark bind to collagen, slow process taking months, produces supple and durable leather, traditional method

name: Chrome tanning: chromium salt curing
note: Chromium sulfate rapidly tans hides, produces softer leather than vegetable tanning, faster but requires chemical control

name: Alum tanning: mineral salt curing
note: Tanning hides with alum (a mineral salt of aluminium) and common salt in a pickle instead of with plant extracts. It is much faster than vegetable tanning, but the leather is less durable, and washes out in water, so it is mostly used for light leather goods such as gloves. It needs alum and a vat. The leather is white, soft and thin.

name: Currying: leather finish dressing
note: Currying is the finishing of leather after tanning: it is worked and dressed with oil and grease so it becomes supple, waterproofed and of even thickness and colour. It is an essential finishing step before leather can be made into goods. It needs oils or tallow, tools to scrape and stretch the hide, and skilled workers. Poorly curried leather cracks.

name: Splitting: leather layering
note: Controlled splitting of a prepared hide into grain and flesh layers with a guided knife. This is a leather-finishing process, not the much later powered band-knife splitter.

name: Embossing: surface pattern pressing
note: Pressing a pattern into the surface of leather with a hot press and a pattern die, creating a texture. It replicates the look of natural grain or adds decoration. Mechanical equipment made it faster. It needs engraved dies made to fine tolerance, and a heated press. Too much heat scorches the leather, and too little leaves a faint pattern.

name: Lasting machine: shoe fitting
note: A machine for pulling the upper leather of a shoe tightly over a wooden last (a foot-shaped form) and holding it while the sole is attached. Pneumatic or mechanical clamps do the work, and the tension is maintained while nails fix the sole. It replaces skilled hand work. It needs tolerance machining and pneumatic or lever parts. Uneven pulling gives a misshapen shoe.

name: Mechanised shoemaking: factory production
note: Chain of specialized machines and workers, division of labour, higher speed and lower cost, emerged in America mid-1800s

name: Rubber soles: vulcanised footwear
note: Vulcanised rubber soles reduce cost and improve water resistance, attached by cements or nailing, increasingly common from 1890s

name: Safety match: controlled ignition
note: Phosphorus on match strip, ignition requires friction on box strip, much safer than friction matches, Swedish invention 1844

name: Friction match: white phosphorus tip
note: White phosphorus mixed with oxidiser at stick tip, ignites spontaneously in air, dangerous but widespread in 19th century

name: Safety razor: guarded blade shaving
note: Thin steel blade held in guard, Gillette patent 1901, replaceable blade and guard system, transformed male grooming

name: Razor blade: replaceable steel cutting
note: A thin blade of hardened steel, stamped and honed to a sharp edge, made to be thrown away when it is dull. The business model is a cheap holder with a steady sale of blades to replace. It needs steel that takes a keen edge, precise stamping and sharpening. Blades that are too soft dull quickly; too hard, they chip.

name: Toothbrush: hair bristle cleaning
note: Natural bristles set in wooden handle, Chinese technology known early, mass production in Europe from late 1800s

name: Mass-produced soap: standardised bars
note: Soap made in standard formulation, cut into uniform bars, wrapped and branded, so it can be sold widely instead of being made locally. It transformed soap into a mass-market good. It needs hard soap from oil and lye (an alkali solution), and a kiln for heat. Consistent quality, packaging and distribution are the difficult parts, more than the chemistry.

name: Shampoo: hair cleansing liquid
note: A liquid soap formulated specifically to clean hair. Plain bar soap leaves scum in hard water and strips the hair. It needs hard soap made from oil and lye, and a heated vessel to dissolve it. Mass production and branding were the key factors in making it a common product.

name: Comb: hair grooming tool
note: A tool for grooming hair, made of horn or bone cut into teeth. It is a traditional technology. Mass production came with celluloid combs, which could be moulded rather than cut. It needs horn or bone, a saw and files. The teeth must be cut evenly and smoothed or they snag hair.

name: Mirror: reflective glass surface
note: A flat glass plate backed with a polished tin or lead-tin reflective layer and sealed from corrosion. The backing process, adhesion, and glass flatness distinguish it from an ancient polished-metal mirror.

name: Button: horn material
note: A button made of horn: a disc is cut from animal horn, softened with heat, shaped, drilled with holes for thread, and its edges finished. It is a traditional high-quality material and has been made since the Middle Ages. It needs horn and tools to saw and drill it. Horn is tough and takes dye.

name: Button: bone material
note: A button made of bone: a disc is carved out of animal bone, drilled with holes for thread and finished. It is fine in quality and durable, and was the standard in the Middle Ages. It needs bone, saws, files and a drill. Bone buttons can crack if the holes are drilled too close to the edge.

name: Button: shell material
note: A button cut from mother-of-pearl or other shell into discs, drilled and polished. The shell is lustrous and a trade commodity moved by water, since it comes from seas and rivers. It needs shell, saws and drills. The supply depends on shell fishing, and shell splits easily if drilled carelessly.

name: Button: celluloid plastic material
note: A button made by pressing or stamping celluloid, an early plastic, softened with heat, into shape. It is cheaper and easier to make than natural materials, and it can be made in any colour. It needs celluloid, which is made from nitrocellulose and camphor, and a heated press. Celluloid is flammable.

name: Pin: sewing fastener
note: A sewing pin: a length of drawn wire sharpened to a point at one end and fitted with a head at the other. It is used to hold cloth together while sewing. Each was made by hand in many separate operations, which was labour-intensive, and pins were made by the thousand in medieval workshops. It needs wire that has been drawn through a die.

name: Hand needle: bone, bronze or drawn iron
note: Hand-sewing needle: a bone sliver, bronze rod or drawn iron wire, pointed on stone and pierced with a drill or punch. Within millimetre workmanship; the steel and machine needles below need the tenth-millimetre rung.

name: Needle: sewing implement
note: A sewing needle: a thin rod of polished iron or steel with an eye at one end. It is the essential tool of hand sewing before sewing machines. It is hand-forged: the wire is cut, pointed, flattened where the eye goes, punched, hardened and tempered, and polished. It needs steel wire and files fine enough to work to a tenth of a millimetre. Needles that are not tempered bend or break.

name: Spectacle frame: eye support structure
note: Horn or metal frame holding optical lenses, nose bridge and arms, emerged in medieval period with mass production in 1800s

name: Watch case: portable timepiece housing
note: A fitted protective housing for an already-built portable watch, with hinged cover, stem opening, crystal seat, and access for winding and service. The case is meaningless before a pocket-watch movement exists; decorative brass, silver, or gold work follows the working timepiece.

name: Fountain pen: reservoir writing
note: Internal ink reservoir and feed system, iridium or gold nib, Waterman patent 1884 creates commercial success, transforms business writing

name: Ballpoint pen: ball-point writing
note: Small steel ball in socket, ink flows as ball rotates, Hungarian invention 1938, mass production challenges overcome by 1950s

name: Pencil: graphite and clay mixture
note: Ground graphite and clay mixed and fired, Conté and others develop proportions and hardness grades

name: Eraser: rubber pencil mark removal
note: A piece of rubber that removes pencil marks by abrasion, picking up graphite particles. Versions are mounted in a cap or on the end of a pencil. It needs natural rubber, cured by heat, and a source of latex. Mass production came with the rubber industry. Rubber perishes with age and hardens, and then smears instead of cleaning.

name: Paperclip: bent wire fastener
note: A paper fastener made of wire bent into overlapping loops, which grips sheets by spring tension. It is simple but effective. It needs drawn wire of springy steel, tempered so it returns to shape, and a bending machine. Mass production made cheap office supplies. A soft wire loses its spring.

name: Stapler: metal wire fastener machine
note: A hand-powered device that drives a metal staple through sheets of paper and bends its legs over to clinch them. A lever pushes the staple, and an anvil folds the legs. It needs precisely machined parts and drawn wire formed into staples. It speeds up office work. A bent or jammed staple stops the machine.

name: Drawing pin: short fastening point
note: A short metal point with a wide flat head, made of brass or steel, which can be pushed by thumb into a board to hold paper in place. It leaves only a small hole when taken out, so it does not permanently damage. It needs drawn wire or stamped sheet and tolerance machining. A badly made pin bends before it enters.

name: Envelope: paper folded container
note: An envelope: paper folded into a pocket and gummed so the flap seals the contents. Folding machines made them in mass production and transformed postal efficiency, because a letter could be sent without wrapping and sealing each time. It needs rag paper and gum. The paper must be cut to a pattern that folds square.

name: Gummed envelope flap: adhesive sealing
note: An adhesive strip along the envelope flap, made of starch paste that dries hard and becomes sticky when moistened. It improves on sealing letters with wax or tape. It needs starch and a kiln or oven to dry it. If it is too weak the envelope opens in the post; if too strong, it is hard to seal.

name: Postcard: prepaid correspondence
note: A thin card with the postage pre-printed on it, offered as a cheap alternative to a letter. It travels open, without an envelope, so the message can be read by anyone. It needs paper, printing and a postal service that accepts it. Mass production of cards followed the postal service's introduction of a cheap rate.

name: Printed playing card: mass-produced game
note: Woodcut cards, faster and cheaper than hand-painted. Creates mass market for cards. High profit because cards wear out and players buy replacements.

name: Board game: printed game on board
note: A printed game board with rules and playing pieces, made in mass production for family entertainment. It needs printed playing card technology, paper and boards, and printing in colour. Families with spare time and money must exist to buy it. Rules must be printed clearly, or the game is not played.

name: Jigsaw puzzle: dissectable picture
note: Printed image on wood or cardboard, hand-sawed or die-cut into interlocking pieces, emerges in 18th century as education and entertainment

name: Doll: articulated child plaything
note: A doll: a child's toy figure with articulated limbs and a face, made from wood or cloth. Mass production with porcelain heads came with factory methods. It needs skilled craftsmen for carving and painting, and tolerance in the joints. Porcelain heads need a kiln; wood and cloth are cheaper but less durable.

name: Tin toy: stamped metal plaything
note: A toy stamped out of thin sheets of tin plate and decorated by lithographic printing, with joints or wheels. Germany and Japan became major producers. It needs tin plate, stamping dies made to fine tolerance and a printing process for the colours. Sharp edges are a risk to children, and rust spoils tin toys in damp.

name: Clockwork toy: spring-driven mechanism
note: A toy driven by a wound spring that turns gears and linkages, making it walk or move. It was a premium toy for the children of wealthy families. It needs spring steel and small gears cut to fine tolerance, as in clockmaking. A spring wound too hard breaks, and the toy runs down quickly.

name: Bicycle: mass-produced consumer good
note: A bicycle: a frame carries two wheels, pedals drive the rear wheel by a chain, and pneumatic (air-filled) rubber tyres cushion the ride. Mass production made it cheap enough for ordinary people and transformed personal transport. It needs tolerance machining for bearings, chains and gears, and vulcanised rubber. Bad tyres and loose bearings make a bicycle hard to ride.

name: Camera: mass-produced photographic device
note: A simple camera sold to the general public, with a fixed-focus lens and loaded with roll film, so the user only points and presses a button; the maker develops the film. It made photography available to the masses. It needs tolerance machining, roll film and a developing service. A low price depends on volume.

name: Gramophone: sound recording reproduction
note: Needle-vibration pickup playing wax cylinder or disc, horn amplification, emerges in 1890s and becomes major consumer product

name: Radio set: wireless receiver entertainment
note: A radio receiver for the home: a crystal set or a valve (vacuum tube) receiver, with a loudspeaker. Mass production made it cheap and changed home entertainment. It needs radio technology, parts made to fine tolerance and a broadcasting service to listen to. Without programmes to broadcast there is no market for sets.

name: Vacuum flask: thermal insulation
note: Double-walled glass with vacuum between, reflective surfaces, Thermos trade name, emerges in 1900s for portable hot beverages

name: Tin can: sealed metal container
note: A sealed can made of rolled and soldered tin plate (iron sheet coated with tin), used to preserve food and other goods. It needs tin plate and soldering. Food inside must be cooked after sealing, so that it keeps; a poor seal lets spoilage in. Early cans were closed by hand, so mass production brought them within reach of ordinary people.

name: Paper bag: folded container
note: A bag of strong kraft paper, folded and glued, with gussets (folded sides) at the bottom for capacity. It replaced cloth sacks for retail goods. It needs rag paper or other strong paper and glue, and a folding machine. A weak bottom seam splits under load.

name: Cardboard box: folded laminate container
note: A box of paper sheets laminated (glued in layers) and folded, replacing wooden crates for many goods. It is cheaper and lighter than wood. It needs paper and glue and a folding or die-cutting step, and tolerance machining. Damp weakens it, so it is not for use where it would get wet.

name: Corrugated box: fluted paper structure
note: A box made from board with a wavy (fluted) paper core between flat faces. The flutes act like many small arches, making it light and strong, and it supports stacking and shipping. It needs paper and a machine to crimp the flutes, made to fine tolerance. It cushions goods better than flat cardboard, but is damaged by water.

name: Bottle: glass container
note: A glass container for liquids, hand-blown at first and later moulded, which seals and preserves its contents. A gather of molten glass is blown into a mould. It needs a furnace that sustains the glass at working temperature. The glass must be annealed (cooled slowly) or the bottle cracks. Moulds made mass production possible.

name: Crown cork: crimped bottle seal
note: Crimped tin cap with cork liner, seals carbonated beverages, bottling machine applies caps, invented 1891

name: Screw cap: threaded closure
note: A closure with a thread that screws onto the grooved neck of a bottle. Unlike a cork it can be removed and replaced, and it seals well. Early caps were of wood and later of metal and plastic. It needs tolerance machining to cut matching threads on both neck and cap. If the thread does not match, it leaks.

name: Tube for toothpaste: extrudable container
note: A collapsible metal tube with a sealed cap, from which the contents are squeezed out. It enables portable toothpaste, paints and ointments, and keeps the contents sealed from air. It needs thin soft metal sheet and tolerance machining for the cap thread. Metal tubes do not return to shape, so the contents cannot be sucked back.

name: Capability: reliable electric motor
note: A stage in the textile tree that stands for having a reliable electric motor to run the machines. It marks that the power supply is available to drive textile machinery. It requires local electric power. Without a steady supply, motor-driven machines run unevenly or stop.
